lesson.title: Trust-Busting: Reviving the Sherman Antitrust Act as a Real Weapon
lesson.summary: Trust-busting refers to the federal government's use of antitrust lawsuits, revived under Theodore Roosevelt and continued under William Howard Taft, to break up or restrain monopolistic corporate combinations, most famously the Northern Securities Company in 1904 and Standard Oil in 1911.
lesson.body:
Congress had passed the Sherman Antitrust Act back in 1890, outlawing contracts, combinations, and conspiracies that restrained trade or created monopolies, but for its first decade the law was enforced weakly and interpreted narrowly. In an 1895 case, United States v. E.C. Knight Co., the Supreme Court had ruled that manufacturing was not itself commerce and therefore largely beyond the reach of the Sherman Act, a decision that left huge industrial combinations, the trusts that had multiplied during the Gilded Age, mostly untouched by federal law. By the time Theodore Roosevelt took office in 1901, trusts controlled enormous shares of industries from oil to steel to railroads, and the muckraking journalism of writers like Ida Tarbell had built public awareness of how those combinations had been assembled, often through practices that were plainly unfair even if the law had not yet caught up.

Roosevelt's approach was not to oppose bigness in business as such. He drew a distinction between what he considered good trusts, large firms achieving efficiency through legitimate competition, and bad trusts that used predatory tactics, secret rebates, or outright fraud to crush rivals and gouge consumers, and he wanted government strong enough to tell the difference and act on it. His administration's most consequential early case targeted the Northern Securities Company, a giant railroad holding company organized in 1901 by financier J.P. Morgan along with railroad magnates James J. Hill and E.H. Harriman to combine control of major competing rail lines in the Northwest. Roosevelt's Justice Department sued to dissolve it, and in 1904 the Supreme Court ruled five to four in Northern Securities Co. v. United States that the combination violated the Sherman Act, a decision that startled the business world and established that the law had real teeth after all.

Roosevelt's administration filed more than forty antitrust suits over his time in office, part of the broader Square Deal promise of a government that would police corporate power rather than simply defer to it. The trust-busting campaign did not end with Roosevelt. His chosen successor, William Howard Taft, is sometimes overlooked in this story, but Taft's administration actually filed more antitrust suits than Roosevelt's had, and it was under Taft, not Roosevelt, that the Supreme Court in 1911 ordered the breakup of Standard Oil, the very monopoly Ida Tarbell had documented years earlier, along with the American Tobacco Company in the same year.

Trust-busting never eliminated large corporations from American life, and it was not meant to. What it established was the principle that the federal government had both the legal authority and the political will to intervene when corporate combinations crossed from efficient scale into monopoly power that harmed competitors and consumers, a principle that has shaped American antitrust policy ever since.
